b.bio: Ouen of Rouen (c. c. 609–684) — Audoin (Audoenus, Dado), born at Sancy near Soissons around 609 and died at Clichy on 24 August (683 per the Catholic Encyclopedia; 684 per Wikipedia and Encyclopedia.com), was educated at the Abbey of Saint-Médard de Soissons and served Dagobert I as referendary or chancellor. He founded the monastery of Rebais (c. 634–635) and was consecrated bishop of Rouen on 13 May 641, promoting monasticism notably at Fontenelle while remaining involved in public affairs under the mayor Ebroïn. A close friend of Eligius of Noyon from their years at court, he wrote the Vita Sancti Eligii after his friend's death.
b.s: The library holds his Life of Saint Eligius — an important source for the life of Eligius and for seventh-century Neustrian episcopal life — together with a sermon, verses, and letters.

b.bio:
Constantine I (272–337) — Flavius Valerius Constantinus, Roman emperor from 306 to 337 and the first emperor to convert to Christianity. He legalized Christian practice through the Edict of Milan (313), funded church building, summoned the Council of Nicaea (325), and founded Constantinople as a new capital. Born at Naissus, son of Constantius Chlorus and Helena. The library holds only an eight-page Appendix from Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 8, a collection of pieces printed under his name; the attribution of such appendix material to the emperor himself is doubtful. A later Pope Constantine (consecrated 708, d. 715) is a distinct person and not this author.

John (unknown) — The library prints this author simply as 'John' on its Latin Fathers shelf, holding one work: an eight-page Appendix in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 8. No source passage or library-record evidence confirms which 'John' this is. The candidate Johns in the sources — John of Damascus (c. 675–749), John Balbi (d. c. 1298), Dominican grammarian of Genoa, and John of Fécamp (d. 1079), abbot of Fécamp — cannot be matched to this record: the shelf is explicitly Latin Fathers, while John of Damascus was a Byzantine/Greek father whose works appear in the Patrologia Graeca, so the Damascus identification contradicts the record and the Damascus sources are set aside.
b.s: The works under his name here are minor appendix items in PL 8; Constantine matters to readers of patristic theology chiefly as the emperor whose patronage shaped the fourth-century church.

b.bio: Jerome (c. c. 342–420) — Eusebius Sophronius Hieronymus, born at Stridon on the border of Dalmatia and Pannonia around 342–347, died at Bethlehem on 30 September 420. Baptized in Rome, he studied in Trier and Aquileia, then traveled east: Antioch, the desert of Chalcis (374–379), Constantinople, then Rome from 382 to 385 as secretary to Pope Damasus I. After Damasus's death, enemies of his harsh tongue forced him out; he settled at a monastery in Bethlehem in 386 and remained there until his death. He was ordained a priest at Antioch. His life's work was Scripture: a Latin Old Testament translated from the Hebrew rather than the Septuagint (the translation later called the Vulgate), commentaries spanning the prophets and Gospels, and polemics against Jovinian, Rufinus, and Origenist teaching.
b.s: The works held here are his Hebrew-based biblical scholarship — commentaries on Isaiah, Ezekiel, Jeremiah, the Minor Prophets, Job, Matthew, and Pauline epistles, plus letters and anti-Jovinian polemic — grounded in his thesis that the Hebrew text corrects Septuagint errors.

b.bio: The 'Uncertain author of Melk' (conventionally known as the *Anonymus Mellicensis*) is the designation for the 12th-century Benedictine monk who authored a continuation of the patristic literary catalogs. Though traditionally associated with the Benedictine Abbey of Melk in Austria where the manuscript was preserved, modern scholarship widely identifies the writer as Wolfger of Prüfening. Writing around 1135, he produced a comprehensive bio-bibliographical treatise modeling the earlier works of Jerome, Gennadius, and Isidore of Seville. The compilation preserves vital contemporary information on roughly 120 ecclesiastical writers spanning late antiquity to the twelfth century.
b.s: He compiled *De scriptoribus ecclesiasticis*, a fundamental medieval literary history that documents the transmission and canon of patristic and early medieval theology.

b.bio: The uncertain author of Zwettl is an anonymous writer catalogued within the Latin Fathers tradition as the author of the History of the Roman Pontiffs.
b.s: The author is cited in historical collections for preserving medieval chronicles and papal records associated with the manuscript tradition of Zwettl Abbey.

w: On the Translation of St. Stephen

b.bio: Anastasius Bibliothecarius (c. 810–c. 878) — Anastasius Bibliothecarius, born about 810, was a nephew of Bishop Arsenius of Orte and learned Greek from Eastern monks, making him among the most learned ecclesiastics of ninth-century Rome. He became cardinal priest of St. Marcellus about 848, was deposed in 853 for political activity, and stood briefly as antipope against Benedict III in 855 before being reconciled. Under Nicholas I he served as abbot of Santa Maria in Trastevere and ghost-wrote much papal correspondence; Adrian II appointed him librarian of the Roman Church, and in 869 he went to Constantinople as envoy of Emperor Louis II, arriving during the Eighth Ecumenical Council.
b.s: The works held here present him as a compiler of Frankish history and relic narratives: an abbreviated history of the Franks asserting that papal authority may depose and appoint kings and that Charles Martel was damned for despoiling the church, and an account of the translation of St. Stephen defending relics that expel demons and work healing miracles.

b.bio: Dionysius Exiguus (c. 470 – c. 544) — Dionysius Exiguus ('the Humble') was a monk born in Scythia Minor (modern Romania) who lived in Rome from around 500 until his death before 544. Cassiodorus calls him a Scythian, learned in both Greek and Latin; later writers honor him as an abbot, though Cassiodorus describes him as still an ordinary monk late in life. He translated 401 church canons from Greek into Latin — the Apostolic Canons, Nicaea, Constantinople, Chalcedon, Sardica — and compiled the decretals of popes from Siricius to Anastasius II. His Collectiones canonum Dionysianae carried great authority in the West. At Pope John I's request he prepared in 525 the Easter reckoning that introduced Anno Domini dating. The works here include his canonical collections and Easter letters alongside his Latin translations: Gregory of Nyssa on the creation of man, the Life of Pachomius, and the finding of John the Baptist's head. A Synodal Letter is also held under his name, though some works long attributed to him (e.g. Cyril of Alexandria's synodical letter) are now assigned to Marius Mercator.
b.s: The works held here are the foundations of Western canon law and the Easter computus that gave the Christian calendar its AD numbering.

The works here include his canonical collections and Easter letters alongside his Latin translations: Gregory of Nyssa on the creation of man, the Life of Pachomius, and the finding of John the Baptist's head. A Synodal Letter is also held under his name, though some works long attributed to him (e.g. Cyril of Alexandria's synodical letter) are now assigned to Marius Mercator.

Cyril of Alexandria (c. 376–444) — Cyril was Patriarch of Alexandria from 412 until his death in 444, succeeding his uncle Theophilus. He led the Alexandrian church at the height of its influence in the Roman Empire and became a central figure in the Christological controversy against Nestorius, Patriarch of Constantinople. At the Council of Ephesus (431) Nestorius was deposed; the opposing Nestorian bishops at their rival synod condemned Cyril as a heretic. His career also included the expulsion of Novatians and Jews from Alexandria, and historians still debate his responsibility for tensions surrounding the murder of Hypatia.
b.s: The works held here are the foundations of Western canon law and the Easter computus that gave the Christian calendar its AD numbering.

b.bio: Einhard (c. 770–840) — Einhard (also Eginhard), born around 770 in the Maingau, was educated at Fulda and entered Charlemagne's court around 791, where he worked on palace construction at Aachen and Ingelheim. Louis the Pious made him his private secretary in 814; he managed Charlemagne's will and helped facilitate Louis's elevation as co-emperor. He retired from court during the disputes among Louis's sons and died on 14 March 840 at Seligenstadt. Sources give his birth year as c. 770 (Britannica) or c. 775 (Wikipedia); the wider range covers both.
b.s: His Vita Karoli Magni is the principal contemporary biography of Charlemagne, and the works here also include annals of Lorsch, letters, charters, a rhythm on the passion of Marcellinus and Peter, and an account of the translation of the martyrs Marcellinus and Peter.

b.bio: Godfrey of Saint Victor (c. c. 1125–1190) — Godfrey of Saint Victor (Geoffrey, Godefridus) studied and taught the trivium at Paris under Adam of Balsham (1144–1155), possibly studied law at Bologna, and then entered the Abbey of Saint-Victor in Paris before 1160. After Richard of Saint Victor's death in 1173, Prior Walter drove him from the abbey to a rural priory around 1180, where he wrote his principal work, the Microcosmus; he returned to Saint-Victor after Walter's death (c. 1190) and served as sacristan until his death. He is to be distinguished from Godfrey of Breteuil, a separate figure of the same century.
b.s: One of the last major Victorines, he carried Hugh and Richard's mystical tradition into a Christian humanism that classified knowledge and defended the study of ancient philosophy; his Microcosmus survives in an autograph manuscript with self-portraits.

b.bio: Jerome (c. c. 342–420) — Eusebius Sophronius Hieronymus, born at Stridon on the border of Dalmatia and Pannonia around 342–347, died at Bethlehem on 30 September 420. Baptized in Rome, he studied in Trier and Aquileia, then traveled east: Antioch, the desert of Chalcis (374–379), Constantinople, then Rome from 382 to 385 as secretary to Pope Damasus I. After Damasus's death, enemies of his harsh tongue forced him out; he settled at a monastery in Bethlehem in 386 and remained there until his death. He was ordained a priest at Antioch. His life's work was Scripture: a Latin Old Testament translated from the Hebrew rather than the Septuagint (the translation later called the Vulgate), commentaries spanning the prophets and Gospels, and polemics against Jovinian, Rufinus, and Origenist teaching.
b.s: The works held here are his Hebrew-based biblical scholarship — commentaries on Isaiah, Ezekiel, Jeremiah, the Minor Prophets, Job, Matthew, and Pauline epistles, plus letters and anti-Jovinian polemic — grounded in his thesis that the Hebrew text corrects Septuagint errors.

b.bio: John the Subdeacon (unknown) — The library holds one short work under this name, 'Sayings of the Elders' (PL 73, 15pp), a collection of monastic sayings treating sin, prayer, sanctification, last things, virtues, grace, eternal life, angels, providence, and true worship, citing figures such as Ruff, Pasch, Abbot Macarius, Abbot Pastor, Cyrion, and the fathers of Scetis, and arguing against a certain philosopher and against the devil. Nothing further about this author is supported by the supplied evidence.
b.s: His 'Sayings of the Elders' transmits desert-father teaching on sin, prayer, sanctification, and virtue as received in Latin monastic circles.

b.bio: Martin of Braga (c. 520–580) — Born in Pannonia about 520, Martin became a monk in the Holy Land and came to Gallaecia around 550 to convert the Suevi, some still pagan or Arian. He founded monasteries, including Dumio, where he was abbot and then bishop, signing the Synod of Braga of 561 as Bishop of Dumio. He later became Archbishop of Braga and presided over the second Council of Braga in 572. Gregory of Tours called him second to none of his contemporaries in learning. He died at Braga in 580; his feast is 20 March.
b.s: The works held here are his moral and ascetical treatises — on anger, pride, humility, honest living — which provided an influential model for the religious instruction that shaped the later conversion of northern and eastern Europe.

b.bio: Paschasius the Deacon (d. c. 512) — A deacon of the Roman Church active around 500, known almost entirely through Gregory the Great's Dialogues (IV, 40), which calls him a man of great sanctity and a father of the poor. He supported the antipope Laurentius until his death, an adherence Gregory attributes to error rather than malice; he died during the pontificate of Symmachus, around 512 or shortly after. Gregory reports posthumous appearances to Bishop Germanus of Capua and praises books on the Holy Spirit left by him as correct and lucid. Two books De spiritu sancto are assigned to him in manuscripts and printed in PL 62, though Engelbrecht attributed them instead to Faustus of Riez.
b.s: The library's On the Holy Spirit is the two-book treatise defending the Spirit's full deity against Macedonian denial (and against Arian denials), the work Gregory commended; the Sayings of the Elders and Prologue from PL 73 are monastic material printed under his name but of doubtful relation to the Roman deacon.

b.bio: An uncertain author tentatively associated with Paul the Deacon in library cataloguing records, associated with the Latin Fathers tradition as the attributed author of the Passion of St. Cyprian and the Life and Miracles of St. Arnulf.
b.s: Represents an uncertain or disputed hagiographical attribution in early Christian manuscript and catalogue traditions for texts regarding Saint Cyprian and Saint Arnulf.

b.bio: Pelagius the Deacon (c. 500–561) — The library prints this author as 'Pelagius the Deacon,' and the biographical sources identify him with Pelagius of Rome, born into a noble Roman family around 500 and pope from 16 April 556 until his death on 3 March 561. As a deacon he accompanied Pope Agapetus I to Constantinople in 536 and was appointed apocrisiarius there, acquiring influence with Justinian I; he returned to Rome in 543 and stayed as Pope Vigilius's representative during Totila's blockade of the city. He first opposed Justinian's condemnation of the Three Chapters, then adopted the emperor's position, and his pontificate was marked by the schism that followed the Council of Constantinople. A Latin collection of monastic sayings ('Sayings of the Elders') is transmitted under the name 'Pelagius the Deacon' and is the work held here; the sources consulted do not themselves connect this compilation to the future pope, so its attribution rests on the library record alone.
b.s: The work here is a Latin collection of desert monastic sayings — teaching on prayer, continence, humility, and dying to self — transmitted under the name of a deacon identified with the man who later became pope amid the Three Chapters controversy.

w: Continuation of the Chronicle of Saint Benignus

b.bio: This heading represents anonymous and uncertain authors catalogued under the Latin Fathers tradition whose attributed writings include the Chronicle of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon, its continuation, liturgical works, hymns, and prolegomena.
b.s: These anonymous medieval writings preserve liturgical material, hymns, and monastic historical records associated with the Abbey of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon.

b.bio: Ulrich was born at Kyburg in present-day Switzerland, educated at St. Gall, and consecrated Bishop of Augsburg on 28 December 923 under King Henry I. He reformed the clergy through visitations and church-building, held Augsburg against the Magyars in 955 before Otto I's victory at the Lechfeld, made three pilgrimages to Rome, and founded the nunnery of St. Stephen. He died at Augsburg on 4 July 973 and was canonized by Pope John XV in 993 — the first saint canonized by a pope rather than a local authority.
b.s: The library holds a single charter printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina 135, touching on the Church and true worship; it is a documentary witness to his episcopal administration rather than a theological treatise.

b.bio: The name as printed does not correspond to any figure The surviving records describe. The Tegernsee monks documented here are Metellus (fl. 1145–1165), poet of the Expeditio Hierosolymitana, and Werner the Scholasticus (d. after 1195), head of the abbey school; neither is credited with letters on clerical discipline. Ulrich of Zell (c. 1029–1093) was a Cluniac reformer of Regensburg origin, not a Tegernsee author. What can be said comes from the works themselves: two pages of letters in PL 141 arguing that notorious sins disqualify a cleric from ministry, that consent to sin makes one guilty with the doer, and that unfit clerics must be canonically deposed by synodal judgment.
b.s: The letters held here are a brief polemic against one Raherius over the removal of unfit clerics, insisting that eternal peril outweighs temporal loss and that bribery cannot excuse injustice.

w: Double Epitaph of Marbod of Rennes
Report for the Monastery of Roda

b.bio: Ulger (Ulgerius) was Bishop of Angers from 1125 until his death in 1148 or 1149, succeeding Rainald de Martigné and continuing the Gregorian reform in his diocese. A student of Marbod of Rennes and his successor as archdeacon, he composed a eulogy/epitaph for his teacher. His episcopate was marked by litigation: against Glanfeuil Abbey shortly after his elevation, then a long dispute with Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, pleaded before Pope Innocent II in consistory around 1136, and from the 1140s a conflict with Fontevraud Abbey over bridges and tolls that drew rebuke from Bernard of Clairvaux and led Innocent II to suspend him in 1142.
b.s: The works here are legal-polemical pieces from his jurisdictional disputes—reports, letters, and epitaphs arguing that papal confirmation secures ecclesiastical grants, that long possession establishes right to a chapel, and that judgments procured without due summons are void.

b.bio: Uranius was a Gaul by birth and a presbyter of the church at Nola, a friend of Paulinus of Nola who was present at his death in 431. Shortly after that death he wrote an account of it at the request of Pacatus, addressed to one preparing to versify Paulinus' life. The letter recounts Paulinus' final communion with bishops Symmachus and Acindynus, visions of Martin of Tours and Ianuarius before his death, and an appearance after death to a bishop of Naples. It survives as Epistula Uranii presbyteri de obitu s. Paulini ad Pacatum (BHL 6558), printed in PL 53.
b.s: The single work held here is the primary eyewitness account of how Paulinus of Nola died, and it asserts that departed saints pray for the living and are received by fellow saints — themes of early Latin piety toward the dead.

b.bio: Uberto Crivelli, a Milanese of the noble Crivelli family, was created a cardinal by Lucius III and became archbishop of Milan in 1185; on the day Lucius died at Verona, 25 November 1185, he was elected pope in his place. His pontificate was consumed by conflict with Emperor Frederick Barbarossa over episcopal appointments and imperial influence, embittered by personal enmity dating to the sack of Milan in 1162, when the emperor had several of the pope's relatives proscribed or mutilated. He died at Ferrara on 20 October 1187, shortly after news of Hattin reached Europe; Gregory VIII proclaimed the Third Crusade in his place.
b.s: The volume held here is his register of letters and privileges, which shows the papal chancery defending tithes, monastic rights, church property, and clerical immunity against lay magnates — including Emperor Frederick and Baldwin, archbishop of Canterbury.

b.bio: Utho (Udo) of Strasbourg, called Argentinensis, was bishop of Strasbourg from 950 until his death in 965. He wrote a Vita of Saint Arbogast, an earlier bishop of the same see, and some later authors also credited him with a lost Vita of Saint Amand of Strasbourg. The library holds only the Arbogast vita, printed in PL 134.
b.s: His one surviving work here is a hagiographic life of Arbogast that presents the saint's healings, exorcisms, and continuing patronage through Mary's intercession, modeling how a tenth-century bishop promoted his see's cults.
